background.definition: Alcoholic hepatitis is part of the spectrum of alcoholic liver disease (alcoholic steatosis, alcoholic hepatitis, and cirrhosis). Alcoholic steatohepatitis is a histologic diagnosis made in patients with elevated transaminases and a history of chronic alcohol use. Alcoholic hepatitis generally refers to the development of acute symptoms related to worsening toxic and inflammatory processes within the liver.

list.listitem: Approximately 10% to 35% of heavy drinkers (ie, those who drink 5-6 standard alcoholic drinks daily) develop alcoholic hepatitis.
Alcoholic hepatitis contributed to 0.8% of all hospitalizations in the US, with 326,000 hospital admissions in 2010.
In 2010, the average cost of hospitalization in the US related to a primary diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis was over $46,000 with a total cost to the healthcare system of over $15 billion.
In the United States, alcoholic liver disease was responsible for over 29,000 deaths in 2020.
Alcohol consumption.
The process is accelerated by coinfection with hepatitis C.

Fatty liver can occur within a few days of heavy drinking and is reversible with cessation. Increased usage leads to early fibrosis and inflammation (alcoholic steatohepatitis). Continued drinking can cause irreversible fibrosis and cirrhosis.
The pathophysiology of alcoholic hepatitis is not completely understood. Alcohol may be a direct hepatotoxin, but not all heavy drinkers develop alcoholic hepatitis.
Genetic factors, free radical formation, metabolic factors, and immune factors (IL-8 and TNF-alpha) have been implicated.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Quantity and pattern of alcohol ingested
Female gender (requires less alcohol consumption for disease)

list.listitem: Screening and behavioral counseling interventions are recommended to reduce alcohol misuse by adults, including pregnant women.B
Brief advice from a primary care physician can reduce alcohol intake in problem drinkers.B
However, brief interventions in inpatients with problem drinking are not effective in reducing alcohol use.B
In patients with compensated alcoholic liver disease, medications such as acamprosate, naltrexone, bacloen, gabapentin, or topiramate are options for treatment of alcohol use disorder.B

list.listitem: Patients predominantly present with new onset or acutely worsening jaundice but may report fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and/or fatigue.

On examination patients may have tender hepatomegaly, ascites, splenomegaly, telangiectasias, palmar erythema, Dupuytren's contractures, peripheral neuropathy, excessive bruising and bleeding, or hepatic encephalopathy.

Since heavy alcohol use is a major characteristic in patients with alcoholic hepatitis, assessing its presence is important. Clues to alcohol use disoder include psychosocial consequences, such as a history of DUI or trauma. The AUDIT is a validated tool to aid in the diagnosis of alcohol use disorder.
In the absence of confounding factors, a liver biopsy is low yield for a clinical diagnosis of probable alcoholic hepatitis.
A CRP level >19 mg/L in heavy drinkers with elevated transaminases and negative hepatitis and HIV serology is helpful at ruling in alcoholic hepatitis.
The AST/ALT ratio is 2 or more times the ULN in 80% of patients with alcoholic hepatitis but is rarely more than 10 times the ULN. Jaundice occurs in 60% to 70% of patients with alcoholic hepatitis.
The severity should be evaluated by measuring serum bilirubin, creatinine, INR, albumin, and electrolytes to calculate the MELD score.
The diagnosis is usually made by the history of significant alcohol use, stigmata of liver disease, and suggestive laboratory data.
Mild to moderate cases of alcoholic hepatitis need only symptomatic and supportive care; alcohol abstinence is the cornerstone of treatment. C

Because they may decrease short term mortality, corticosteroids should be considered in severe cases of alcoholic hepatitis (discriminant function score >32 or MELD score >20) () for patients with no contraindications and good outpatient follow-up. Corticosteroids should be discontinued if the Lille score is not favorable after seven days of treatment. See for a recommended treatment algorithm. B

Evidence for benefit of pentoxifylline in severe alcoholic hepatitis is very weak and therefore the drug is no longer recommended as first line treatment. It may beneficial in a subset of patients with hepatorenal syndrome. B
Supplemental nutrition is recommended in patients who are malnourished. A
Milk thistle, antioxidants, SAMe, amlodipine, colchicine, propylthiouracil, anabolic steroids, prophylactic antibiotics and insulin/glucagon infusions are ineffective. B
See for a summary of guideline-based pharmacologic treatments and potential options with additional research required.

Because they may decrease mortality, corticosteroids (prednisolone 40 mg/day for 4 weeks followed by tapering) are recommended by ACG 2024 guidelines for patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis or in the presence of hepatic encephalopathy. A discriminant function score greater than 32 predicts a 50% mortality and is an indication for steroids (). Thirty-day mortality is lower in patients treated with prednisolone than in those treated with a broad-spectrum antioxidant compound (30% vs 46%; NNT = 7).
The efficacy of steroids in severe disease has not been established in cases of coexisting pancreatitis, gastrointestinal bleeding, renal failure, or active infection.

An individual patient meta-analysis identified 5 RCTs with 417 patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis randomized to corticosteroids or placebo, and found higher 28 day survival with active treatment (80% vs 66%, p <0.005, NNT = 7). However, an updated meta-analysis (not individual patient) found no clear benefits and was critical of the quality of included studies.
In addition, recent Cochrane review calls into question the utility of corticosteroids in the treatment of alcoholic hepatitis.
Adding pentoxifylline to prednisolone does not improve survival compared to steroids alone in severe alcoholic hepatitis.
A large RCT showed that prednisolone or pentoxfylline did not improve outcomes significantly at 1, 3, and 12 months in patients with severe disease.
The addition of N-acetylcysteine to prednisonlone improves short-term but not long-term survival in hospitalized patients with severe disease.

The addition of prophylactic amoxicillin-clavulanate to steroids does not decrease mortality in patients hospitalized with severe alcohol-related hepatitis compared with steroids alone (17% amoxiclav vs 21% placebo, p = 0.33).

ACG 2018 guidelines note that evidence regarding pentoxifyline is inconsistent with mixed results regarding mortality in patients with severe disease. They do note a consistent benefit in terms of renal function and survival in patients with hepatorenal syndrome.

In the seminal short-term study on the drug, 24% of patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis treated with pentoxifylline (400 mg 3 times daily) died compared with 46% of control patients (NNT = 5; 95% CI, 3-34). However, a subsequent Cochrane review of 5 trials concluded that pentoxifylline may have a positive effect on all-cause morbidity and mortality in patients with hepatorenal syndrome, but is associated with an increase in serious and nonserious adverse events; 4 of 5 studies had a high risk of bias risking overstimation of a treatment effect.

A small study (N = 46) showed improvement in 90 day survival (78% vs 30%, p = 0.001, NNT = 2) for patients with severe disease randomized to G-CSF 5μg/kg SC x 5 d or standard treatment with pentoxifylline. However, survival rates for the pentoxifylline group were much lower than those in other trials for that drug.
Infliximab in combination with steroids increases the number of severe infections (NNH = 2; 95% CI, 1-5).
Anabolic-androgenic steroids, propylthiouracil, colchicine, and amlodipine are not beneficial. While early studies raised optimism, glucagon and insulin infusions are ineffective.

A study randomized 292 patients hospitalized with alcoholic hepatitis to prednisolone + amoxiiclav or prednisolone + placebo. At 2 months infection rates were lower (29.7% vs 41.5%, p < 0.05) but mortality was unchanged (17% amoxiclav vs 21% placebo, p = 0.33).

Based on limited data, a systematic review concluded that a variety of treatments have some evidence of effectiveness to treat muscle cramps associated with cirrhosis. The authors favored methocarbamol, orphenadrine, and taurine, though a number of other treatments also decreased cramp frequency.

Although the role of liver transplantation in alcoholic hepatitis remains controversial, a recent surgical pilot of carefully selected patients showed excellent short-term survival and similar rates of resumption of alcohol use compared to patients with 6 months of abstinence.
Two systematic reviews found evidence of reduced mortality following transplantation for carefully selected patients with alcoholic hepatitis.
A systematic review of 11 studies found a risk of alcohol relapse following transplant of 22% for all patients and 14% in patients with clinically severe alcoholic hepatitis.
The evidence supporting the use of milk thistle in alcoholic hepatitis is poor; it appears to be ineffective in decreasing mortality or preventing complications.
Vitamin E does not improve liver function tests in patients with moderate to severe disease.
SAMe has no significant effect on mortality, liver-related mortality, liver transplantation, or liver complications in patients with alcoholic liver disease.
Supportive care and abstinence from alcohol is all that is necessary for patients with mild disease.
Patients who cannot meet their caloric requirements through normal food intake should receive oral nutritional supplements.
While a study found that hepatocellular cancer risk was lower in patients with alcoholic cirrhosis who continued hazardous drinking, that was because their overall mortality was higher.

Branched chain amino acid formulations are recommended for patients who develop hepatic encephalopathy during enteral nutrition; they can also improve clinical outcomes in advanced cirrhosis. Whole protein formulas are recommended for other patients.
Consider more concentrated energy supplements in patients with ascites.

Tube feedings are recommended in patients who are unable to maintain adequate oral intake. Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube placement is associated with higher risk of complications and is not routinely recommended.

Artificial support systems are devices that remove toxins (aromatic amino acids and ammonia), synthesize proteins (eg, albumin and coagulation factors), and reverse the inflammatory processes. The strength of the studies is poor, but it appears artificial support systems may improve short-term outcomes in patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure but not in acute liver failure.
General supportive care is indicated in mild to moderate cases.
Corticosteroids are indicated in cases of severe hepatitis.
The patient should be monitored and treated for alcohol withdrawal.
The discriminant function (), the MELD score, and the Glasgow score () predict mortality in alcoholic hepatitis. A
Forty percent of patients will progress to cirrhosis.
Both obesity (HR 2.2) and being underweight (HR 2.4) were associated with increased mortality at 3 months in patients with alcoholic hepatitis.
Forty percent of patients will progress to cirrhosis.
Several clinical decision rules can stratify the severity of alcoholic hepatitis and predict short-term mortality: MELD, Glasgow score (), and discriminant function ().
A discriminant function score greater than 32 predicts a 50% mortality and is an indication for steroids ().
The MELD score and the discriminant function () have equal prognostic value for 90-day mortality.
The Lille score at 7 days is utilized to determine if corticosteroids are continued.
Combining data from MELD score and the Lille score can better predict outcomes of alcoholic hepatitis compared with either model alone.
Serum keratin-18 fragment levels may hold future promise in predicting 90-day mortality and response to corticosteroid treatment.

Among patients presenting with severe acute on chronic alcohol associated hepatitis, those with more severe portal hypertension had worse outcomes. Those with hepatic venous-portal gradient (HVPG) > 20 mm Hg were more likely to have esophageal varices, a higher MELD score, and were more likely to be admitted.
Once aminotransferases show consistent decline, they do not need to be rechecked until clinical recovery is achieved.
